children: The past two years have been a test. Markets climbed to record highs in late 2024, then fell sharply through early 2026-the Nifty 500 Total Return Index (TRI) losing over 20% from peak to trough-before partly recovering ground. For investors in balanced advantage funds (BAFs), navigating that entire episode was to happen almost automatically.

When markets got expensive, the fund would pull back equity. When they fell and became cheap again, the fund would step in and buy. You wouldn't have to do anything. That's the pitch. BAFs or dynamic asset allocation funds (DAAFs) are built to shift between equity and debt as conditions change-dialling up exposure when markets become attractive, pulling it back when valuations stretch.

The manager, guided by a model, does the timing for you. But the recent correction has tested whether that promise holds in practice. As the Nifty 500 Index fell, the question for every BAF investor became: is my fund actually buying this dip, or is it protecting itself from further losses? And if it did buy, did that translate into better returns when markets recovered?

The big shift Whatever differences exist between individual funds, the direction of travel over the past two years has been consistent. BAFs, as a group, became meaningfully more aggressive. According to data available with PrimeInvestor and fund house factsheets, the average net equity allocation of 34 balanced advantage and dynamic asset allocation funds with a track record of at least two years rose from 52.65% in September 2024 to 64.98% in August 2026.

That is a rise of 12.33 percentage points at the category level. By the end of August 2026, BAFs/DAAFs such as Bajaj Finserv and Quant were holding over 80% each of their portfolios in net equity, well above the category average.

What does a rising net equity allocation actually mean? Bhavana Acharya, Co-founder and fund manager at PrimeInvestor, draws a clear distinction between three numbers that often get confused. "The gross equity exposure is the total equity allocation for the fund, and includes open positions and derivatives. The hedged portion, which is through derivatives, effectively neutralises the equity exposure.

The net equity exposure is the difference between the gross equity and the hedged portion-this exposure, therefore, shows how much of the fund's equity allocation is vulnerable to market movements. Higher the hedging, less the risk as less of the portfolio is open to be affected by market movements," she explains. Who moved, and how Not all funds moved in the same direction, or with the same urgency.

Looking at how individual schemes changed their allocations month by month reveals three distinct approaches. Ravi Kumar TV, Director at Gaining Ground Investment Services, frames the central test simply: "If equity markets have fallen, has the fund increased the allocation? If the equity markets were at the top, did the fund call the top?" The aggressive allocators: Funds in this group raised net equity exposure substantially through the period, often during or immediately after market weakness.

LIC MF and HDFC MF are the clearest examples given the scale of their increases. Baroda BNP Paribas Mutual Fund also belongs here, with net equity of around 80.5% in September 2026. Jitendra Sriram, Senior Fund Manager-Equity at Baroda BNP Paribas Mutual Fund, explains: "If you look at the market valuations, they are now below long-term median levels which is what is indicating a green on our model in terms of higher proportion of risk assets.

title: Did your balanced advantage fund buy the dip or miss it?
